I.	Meridian Publications, a mid-sized publishing house based in New Delhi, recently released an
internal audit report detailing the cost structure involved in producing one of its flagship
educational titles for the upcoming academic season. The management sought to examine each
expenditure head as a proportion of the total production budget to identify areas for potential
cost optimisation.
The audit revealed that the Cost of Printing constituted the single largest expenditure,
accounting for 35% of the total production cost, reflecting the company's reliance on premium
printing infrastructure. Advertisement Charges, the second highest component at 18% of total
expenditure, covered multi-platform promotional campaigns conducted to ensure the book's
commercial visibility across retail and digital channels.
The Cost of Paper, representing 16% of total expenditure, had seen a marginal rise compared
to the previous edition owing to increased raw material costs. The company also made Royalty
payments to the author amounting to 15% of the total expenditure, as per the manuscript
acquisition agreement. Binders Charges, covering the physical binding and finishing of each
unit, stood at 12% of total expenditure. Finally, Miscellaneous expenses — comprising minor
overheads and unforeseen operational costs — made up the remaining 4% of the total
production budget.
The board has scheduled a strategic review to explore whether printing volumes or paper
sourcing contracts can be renegotiated for the next print run, given that these two heads alone
account for more than half the total expenditure.

I.	VeloTech Assemblies, a mid-sized cycle manufacturing unit located in an industrial belt near

operates under an internal benchmark of 1,200 cycles per week, which was set by the
management as the minimum threshold for profitable operation. Each cycle manufactured at
the unit is priced at 71,500 at the factory gate.
According to the production log maintained over five consecutive weeks, the factory produced
700 cycles in the 1st week, a figure that fell significantly below the internal benchmark.
Performance improved sharply in the 2nd week, with output rising to 1,400 cycles, more than
doubling the previous week's production. However, the 3rd week witnessed a dip, with only
1,000 cycles produced, followed by a further decline to 900 cycles in the 4th week. The factory
staged a recovery in the 5th week, recording its best performance of the period with 1,600
cycles — the highest weekly output and the only week to exceed the y-axis maximum of 1,600
on the production chart.
The management observed that production remained inconsistent across the period, with the
first and fourth weeks falling considerably below the benchmark while only the second and
fifth weeks managed to surpass it. The finance team was tasked with preparing a revenue
analysis based on these five weeks of production data to present before the board at the next
quarterly review.

Til.	The Supreme Court of India, on 29 January 2026, stayed the implementation of the University
Grants Commission (UGC) (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions)
Regulations, 2026. These regulations were introduced to address caste-based discrimination
and promote inclusivity in higher education institutions across India. However, soon after
their notification, they became the subject of legal challenges and widespread debate.
A key issue raised by the petitioners concerned the definition of "caste-based discrimination"
under Clause 3(c). The regulation defined such discrimination as actions directed only against
members of Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), and Other Backward Classes
(OBC). Critics argued that this limited definition excluded students from the general category
and could violate the principle of equality guaranteed under Article 14 of the Constitution.
Further concerns were raised about the lack of safeguards against misuse. The regulations did
not provide any clear mechanism to address false or malicious complaints. The Court observed
that certain provisions appeared vague and were potentially open to misuse, raising doubts
about their effective implementation.
The regulations trace their origin to the case of Abeda Salim Tadvi v. Union of India, which
highlighted caste-based discrimination in educational institutions. While acknowledging the
importance of addressing such issues, the Court questioned whether the regulations might
unintentionally create further divisions.
As an interim measure, the Court stayed the 2026 regulations and allowed the earlier 2012
framework to continue until further review.
Source: Supreme Court Observer, "Supreme Court stays 2026 UGC Equity Regulations" (2026).

IV.	The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 took the world by surprise and marked a major
turning point in global politics. With the end of one of the two superpowers, the United States
emerged as the dominant force in international relations. This period is often seen as the
beginning of US hegemony, although some of its foundations had already been laid after the
end of the Second World War in 1945. However, the US did not immediately act as a
hegemonic power; it gradually assumed this role over time.
A significant event that highlighted the growing dominance of the US was the First Gulf War.
In August 1990, Iraq invaded Kuwait and annexed it. After diplomatic efforts failed, the
United Nations authorised military action to liberate Kuwait. This was a crucial decision,
especially after years of Cold War deadlock.
The US President George H.W. Bush described this moment as the emergence of a "new world
order." A coalition of around 660,000 troops from 34 countries was formed, but the operation
was largely dominated by the US. Led by American General Norman Schwarzkopf, nearly 75%
of the forces belonged to the US.
Despite strong claims by Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein, Iraqi forces were swiftly defeated and
forced to withdraw from Kuwait, reinforcing US military supremacy.

The protests were led by local groups including the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and the Kargil

carried banners and raised slogans demanding constitutional safeguards to protect Ladakh's

The core demands of the protesters include granting Ladakh statehood and extending the
provisions of the Sixth Schedule, which provides autonomy and special protections to tribal
areas. Since Ladakh became a Union Territory in 2019 after its separation from Jammu and
Kashmir, many residents have expressed concerns over reduced political representation and
lack of legislative powers. www.lawpreptutorial.com

autonomy and the Centre's governance framework. Despite repeated protests and

VII. India has recorded an unprecedented achievement in its defence sector, with exports reaching
an all-time high during the financial year 2025-26. This sharp rise reflects the country's
strengthening capabilities in manufacturing advanced defence equipment and its increasing
acceptance in the global arms market.
The growth in exports indicates a rising international demand for defence products developed
in India, including sophisticated military systems and technologies. Over the years, India has
expanded its reach by supplying defence equipment to a large number of countries, thereby
establishing itself as a reliable partner in the global defence ecosystem.
Both government-owned enterprises and private companies have played a significant role in
this progress. While public sector units continue to dominate the export share, the
participation of private firms has grown steadily, contributing to innovation and
diversification in production. The increasing number of exporters further highlights the
broadening base of the defence industry.
This success is closely linked to the government's focus on promoting domestic manufacturing
and reducing dependence on imports. Policy reforms, ease of doing business, and streamlined
export procedures have created a favourable environment for growth in the sector. Initiatives
aimed at self-reliance have encouraged the development of indigenous technologies and
strengthened the overall defence infrastructure.
The rise in defence exports not only boosts economic growth but also enhances India's strategic
influence at the global level. It demonstrates the country's ambition to become a key player in
defence production and a major contributor to international security cooperation.

IX.	King of kings they called him, and they said, We rejoice in him, we rejoice in his wife and her
beauty; they said, We love this country, and then we said, We love this country. We had to
rejoice in his newborn son, for longer than we ever would a birth in our own family, his
newborn son, in the far-off Palace of Flowers.
Our parents had been told that the oil, the Americans, the English, were part and parcel of the
same thing, with the Shah, against us. Our parents stopped working, took to the streets, and
then went home again; they were afraid of the secret service and they said nothing more, said
nothing against the Shah ever again. Sent us to school and said, “We love this country; now
you love its schools.”
His haughty gaze above the teacher's desk. We learned what we had to learn, got older, and
decided that whatever was written in our schoolbooks, we wanted the opposite. We read Long
live the Shah and thought, Death to the Shah. We heard All work is owed to the king and said,
“The work belongs to the workers.” And when we read, he leads us to prosperity, we spit on his
palaces and on the English and the Americans. We smuggle books, copy them, learn them by
heart, pass them on to the next person and the next. We have read and read and read, kept
quiet at home and made a noise on the streets, cursed our parents and died for our children.
The Shah has gone because he was sick, and the statues have fallen because the people didn't
believe in them.
Source: An extract from The Nights Are Quiet in Tehran by Shida Bazyar, translated by Ruth
Martin

XVII. In criminal law, the distinction between intention, knowledge, and negligence determines not
only the quantum of punishment but the very character of the offense. Intention involves a
conscious, deliberate objective to bring about a specific consequence. Knowledge exists when

XVIII. In contract law, not every statement made during negotiations becomes a binding term of the
contract. A statement may be a mere representation, intended to induce the other party into
entering the agreement, or it may be a contractual promise, breach of which gives rise to
liability irrespective of fraud. The distinction depends on several factors: the importance
attached to the statement, the relative knowledge of the parties, the timing between the
statement and the contract, and whether the statement was reduced into writing. Where one
party possesses special knowledge and the other relies substantially on that assertion, the law
is more inclined to treat the statement as a term rather than casual sales talk.
This distinction has important consequences. If the statement forms part of the contract, its
falsity may amount to breach even where the maker honestly believed it to be true. If it is
merely a representation, the remedy may depend on whether the misstatement was
fraudulent, negligent, or innocent. However, the law also recognizes that exaggerated
commendation, obvious opinion, or statements not intended to be taken literally do not
ordinarily create contractual obligations. Similarly, where the representee independently
verifies the facts or expressly agrees not to rely solely on pre-contractual assertions, the legal
effect of the statement may weaken.
Courts therefore examine not merely what was said, but the commercial setting in which it
was said. The law seeks to protect genuine reliance, but it does not convert every failed
expectation into breach of contract. Much turns on whether the statement was meant to
allocate risk, and whether a reasonable person in that situation would have understood it as
contractually binding.

XIX. A foundational principle of Indian evidence law is the statutory distrust of statements made to
police officers. Sections 25 and 26 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (now Sections 23 and 24 of
the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2028) establish a firm rule: confessions made to a police
officer, or made while in police custody without a Magistrate present, are completely
inadmissible in court. This absolute bar reflects the legislature’s historical recognition of the
risk that individuals in custody might be coerced, tortured, or pressured into making false
confessions.
However, Section 27 (now Section 26 of the BSA) creates a carefully calibrated exception to
this rule, famously known as the "doctrine of confirmation by subsequent events". It dictates
that if a person in police custody provides information that directly leads to the discovery of a
distinct, previously unknown fact-such as the location of a murder weapon or hidden stolen
property-the specific portion of the statement that strictly relates to that discovery becomes
admissible.
The Supreme Court has mandated strict preconditions for this exception: the individual must
be formally accused of an offense, they must be in active police custody, and the physical fact
must be discovered as a direct consequence of their specific disclosure. Crucially, the law only
allows the admission of the information that caused the discovery, not the accompanying
confession of guilt. If an accused says, "I hid the knife I used to kill him in the bushes," only
the statement "I hid the knife in the bushes" is admissible; the confession of the murder itself
remains firmly barred.

XX. International criminal law differentiates atrocities not merely by the scale of the violence, but
by the specific intent and context of the acts. Under the Rome Statute of the International
Criminal Court (ICC), the three primary core crimes are Genocide, Crimes Against Humanity,

intent. To constitute genocide, acts such as killing, causing serious bodily harm, or forcibly

acts like murder, torture, deportation, or apartheid must be committed as part of a
"widespread or systematic attack directed against any civilian population". Unlike war crimes,
crimes against humanity can be prosecuted even if they occur during peacetime or are
committed by a State against its own citizens. The requirement of a "widespread or
systematic" attack ensures that isolated or random acts of violence, however heinous, do not
trigger international jurisdiction. War Crimes (Article 8) are violations of international
humanitarian law, particularly the Geneva Conventions. They are strictly contextual,
